why_this_tool: MCP is the open protocol that separates hosts, clients and servers, so one small server on a laptop lets you practise tool design, discovery, approval and authorization in the form any agent framework can consume.
alternatives: Framework-native tool definitions in LangGraph or Pydantic AI (faster to start, but tied to one framework), provider-specific function calling (no shared server, every host re-implements the integration), plain REST with an OpenAPI description (mature auth and gateways, but no model-oriented discovery), and Temporal (durable execution for long runs, complementary rather than a tool protocol).

setup.do: Install Node.js so you can launch the reference servers and the MCP Inspector from a package runner.
setup.done_when: Asking Node for its version in a terminal prints a version number.

source.title: Connect to local MCP servers - Model Context Protocol

setup.why: Most reference servers and the Inspector are distributed as Node packages, so this runtime is needed even if you write your own server in Python.

setup.do: Choose one official SDK (Python or TypeScript) and note the install instructions for it.
setup.done_when: You have picked one SDK and can name its package and its repository.
setup.why: Every later step uses one SDK to build a server, and staying with one language keeps the path short.

setup.do: Create a project directory with an isolated environment and add the MCP SDK as a dependency.
setup.done_when: The project has a dependency file that lists the MCP SDK and the environment imports it without error.

source.title: Build an MCP server - Model Context Protocol

setup.why: A dedicated environment with declared dependencies is what you will later pin and rebuild from scratch.

setup.do: Install the desktop host application the documentation uses, so you have a real host to connect servers to.
setup.done_when: The host application opens and shows its settings screen where servers are configured.

source.title: Connect to local MCP servers - Model Context Protocol

setup.why: The host owns the model, the clients and the approval prompts, so you need one to see the protocol from the user side.

steps.do: Run one of the reference servers as it is, without writing any code.
steps.done_when: The reference server process starts and stays running, waiting for a client.
steps.why: Seeing a working server first gives you a known-good baseline before you build your own.

steps.do: Read the participants section and sketch which process on your laptop is the host, which is the client and which is the server.
steps.done_when: You have a sketch labelling the host, one client per server, and each server, for the setup from the previous step.
steps.why: The lesson's host, client and server split decides where permissions, connections and tools live, and one client connects to exactly one server.

steps.do: Write your own server with two tools, each with a precise name, a description written for the model and typed parameters.
steps.done_when: Your server file defines two tools and loads without import or syntax errors.

source.title: Build an MCP server - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: Tool design is mostly naming, descriptions and input schemas, because that is all the model sees when it decides what to call.

steps.do: Start your server and connect to it with the MCP Inspector, with server logs going to standard error.
steps.done_when: The Inspector shows your server as connected and lists both of your tools.
steps.why: The Inspector lets you exercise a server without a model in the loop, which is the fastest feedback cycle for tool work.

steps.do: Query the tool list and call one tool from the Inspector, then read the raw JSON-RPC request and response for each.
steps.done_when: You can point at the tools/list response with your schemas and at a tools/call response with your result.
steps.why: Discovery and execution are two separate exchanges, and reading the messages shows exactly what a host hands to the model.

steps.do: Write an output schema for one tool, return structured content that matches it, and make a bad input return a tool error instead of crashing.
steps.done_when: The Inspector shows structured content matching the schema for a good call and an error result for a bad one.
steps.why: Structured results and clear errors let an agent recover in its loop rather than stall or hallucinate a result.

steps.do: Create one prompt on your server that scripts a fixed sequence of steps, then compare it with letting the model pick tools freely for the same task.
steps.done_when: You have run the task both ways and written down where the sequence of calls differed.

source.title: Understanding MCP servers - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: A prompt the user invokes is a fixed workflow, while model-chosen tool calls are an agent loop, and seeing both side by side is the core distinction of the lesson.

steps.do: Configure the filesystem server in the host with one allowed directory, trigger a write action, and deny it once before approving it.
steps.done_when: The denied action left no file behind and the approved action created the file in the allowed directory.

source.title: Connect to local MCP servers - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: Approval gates are enforced by the host, not the server, and you should see both the refusal path and the approved path.

steps.do: Read the MCP Tasks section of the extensions overview and note how it relates to long-running work and how extensions are negotiated.
steps.done_when: You can state in two sentences what the tasks extension is for and what your server would do when a client does not support it.
steps.why: Durable, bounded runs need a way to track work that outlives one request, and you should know what the protocol offers before adding an external workflow engine.

steps.do: Package your server as an installable package and draft the registry metadata for it locally, without publishing anything.
steps.done_when: A built package exists on disk and your draft metadata names that package and its version.

source.title: The MCP Registry - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: A tool catalog is built from registry metadata that points at packages in ordinary package registries, so the two pieces must line up.

steps.do: Reproduce the server from a clean checkout with pinned dependency versions and rerun your Inspector checks as a repeatable test pass.
steps.done_when: A fresh environment built only from the pinned dependency file passes the same tool list and tool call checks.
steps.why: A server that only works in your shell is not a platform component, and the same checks are what a CI job would run on every change.

steps.do: Configure your server for HTTP transport protected by OAuth, using a local authorization server in a container in place of a paid identity provider, and walk the authorization flow.
steps.done_when: A request without a token is rejected as unauthorized and a request with a token from your local authorization server succeeds.
steps.why: Remote servers must validate tokens issued for them specifically, and this is the setup closest to what a shared production tool server looks like.
